title: The Wanamaker in Wolverhampton Colours: Aaron Rai Becomes First Golfer of Indian Heritage to Win a Major
excerpt: A 68-foot eagle, a 107-year English drought broken, and a love story rooted in Indian golf — Aaron Rai's PGA Championship win is a watershed for the diaspora
body:
## A Century in the Waiting

When Aaron Rai lined up a 68-foot eagle putt on the 17th hole at Aronimink Golf Club last Saturday, the weight of history was not at the front of his mind. "I was just trying to get it close," the 31-year-old from Wolverhampton said afterwards, still visibly stunned. The ball tracked across the green, caught the left edge, and dropped. Three strokes clear of Jon Rahm and Alex Smalley, Rai closed with a final-round 65 to finish at nine-under 271 — and in doing so, became the first Englishman to lift the Wanamaker Trophy since Jim Barnes in 1919.

But for millions of Indians watching from living rooms in Mumbai, London, Toronto, and Houston, the stat that mattered more was a different one: Aaron Rai is the first golfer of Indian heritage ever to win a major championship.

## From Wolverhampton to Wanamaker

Rai's parents emigrated from India and Kenya to the English Midlands, where they ran a small business. His father introduced him to golf at a local municipal course — hardly the gilded country-club origin story that the sport's establishment is used to celebrating. Rai turned professional in 2014, ground his way through the European Tour's lower tiers, and won three times on the DP World Tour between 2018 and 2025 before breaking through on the PGA Tour at the 2024 Wyndham Championship.

None of it was smooth. Injuries dogged him through 2025. He entered the PGA Championship ranked outside the world's top 30, priced at 150/1 by most bookmakers. By Sunday evening, he had a five-year PGA exemption and a place in golf history.

## The Gaurika Factor

Behind every improbable run sits a team, and Rai's begins with Gaurika Bishnoi — his wife, his occasional caddie, and, by his own admission, the better short-game player of the two. "She beats me in every chipping contest we have," Rai told reporters at the trophy ceremony, grinning. "Genuinely. She's ridiculous around the greens."

Bishnoi is no hobby golfer. The India-born professional holds eight titles on the Hero Women's Pro Golf Tour and has competed on the Ladies European Tour. The pair met at the 2018 Hero Indian Open in New Delhi, where Bishnoi was supporting her brother, a fellow golfer. Rai's mother, in his telling, played matchmaker. They married in London in July 2025, and Bishnoi served as his caddie at the 2025 Masters Par-3 Contest, where she sank a shot that drew one of the loudest cheers of the day.

Their embrace behind the 18th green on Sunday — captured by Sports Illustrated's cameras and shared tens of thousands of times across Indian social media — was the image of the championship. Two golfers of Indian heritage, one trophy, and a sport that has never looked quite like this before.

## What It Means for Indian Golf

India is not a golfing nation in the way it is a cricketing one. The country has produced exactly one PGA Tour winner before Rai — Arjun Atwal, who won the 2010 Wyndham Championship as a Monday qualifier at age 37. A handful of others, including Anirban Lahiri and Gaganjeet Bhullar, have carved out respectable careers on various tours. But a major? That was the ceiling nobody had cracked.

Rai's win arrives at an inflection point for the sport in India. Hero MotoCorp's sponsorship of the Indian Open and the Asian Tour has brought international-calibre events to New Delhi. The Indian Golf Union has expanded junior development programmes across fifteen states. And increasingly, the diaspora is producing talent that thrives on the global stage — Rai in England, Sahith Theegala and Akshay Bhatia (both of Indian descent) on the PGA Tour in the United States.

"This is going to inspire a generation of kids in India who might pick up a golf club instead of a cricket bat," said former Indian Open champion Shiv Kapur. "Aaron's story — municipal course, working-class family, Indian heritage — that's the story the sport needs."

## The Diaspora Celebrates

Within hours of Rai's final putt dropping, congratulations poured in from an unlikely coalition: the BCCI, the Indian Golf Union, Sachin Tendulkar, and various NRI community organisations across the US and UK. WhatsApp groups in New Jersey and Southall shared clips of the eagle. Golf clubs from Bengaluru to Birmingham reported a spike in inquiries about junior memberships.

For NRI sports fans accustomed to celebrating India's cricket triumphs from afar, Rai's win felt different — more personal, perhaps, because his story mirrors their own. A family that emigrated, built something, and produced a child who excelled in a domain where brown faces are still rare. Rai has said he intends to compete in the Hero Indian Open again, this time as a major champion.

## What's Next

Rai's five-year PGA exemption guarantees him starts at all four majors through 2031. He is expected to compete at the US Open next month and is now a leading contender for the 2027 Ryder Cup — which would make him the first player of Indian heritage to represent Europe in golf's most prestigious team event. His world ranking, which was 34th entering the week, will jump inside the top 15 when the new rankings are published on Monday.

For now, though, the Wanamaker Trophy sits in a home in Florida shared by two professional golfers of Indian descent. The sport, as Rai put it, "just got a little more interesting."
